---
applyTo: "spec/**/*.rb"
---

# Honeybadger specs

- Tag each example where the code reports an error to Honeybadger with `:honeybadger`, e.g. `it "reports the error to Honeybadger when the newsletter service fails", :honeybadger do`. Tag the example, not its `context` or `describe` block. An untagged example fails when the code calls `Honeybadger.notify`.
- In each `:honeybadger` example, check the error and context of each report with `have_received`, e.g. `expect(Honeybadger).to have_received(:notify).with(an_instance_of(Posts::SendNewsletter::ServiceError), context: { post: published_post.to_honeybadger_context })`. You MUST NOT stub `Honeybadger.notify` in a spec, e.g. `allow(Honeybadger).to receive(:notify)`.
- In integration specs, e.g. request and job specs, check a report's record context with the record's own `to_honeybadger_context`, e.g. `context: { post: published_post.to_honeybadger_context }`. You SHOULD NOT write the record's context hash out. Write a record's hash out only in its model spec, and an error's only in the spec for the service or action that builds it, e.g. `NewsletterClient::UnprocessableError` in the `NewsletterClient` spec.
- In unit specs that check a report, e.g. form and action specs, stub `to_honeybadger_context` on the record's `instance_double` with a small hash and check that the report passes it on, e.g. `instance_double(Post, to_honeybadger_context: { id: 1 })` then `context: { post: { id: 1 } }`.
- Check a model's `to_honeybadger_context` in its model spec in a `describe "#to_honeybadger_context"` block, matching the whole hash with `eq`, e.g. `created_at = Time.zone.now` and `comment = described_class.new(id: 1, locked: false, created_at:, post: Post.new(id: 2, title: "Hello World"))` then `expect(comment.to_honeybadger_context).to eq(id: 1, locked: false, created_at:, post_id: 2, post_title: "Hello World")`. Add an example for each association it reads with `&.`, with the record missing, e.g. `comment = described_class.new(post_id: 2)` then `expect(comment.to_honeybadger_context).to include(post_id: 2, post_title: nil)`.
- When a service's or action's error defines its own `to_honeybadger_context`, check the whole hash with `eq` in that spec's example for each error, in the block passed to `raise_error`, e.g. `.to raise_error(described_class::UnprocessableError) do |error|` then `expect(error.to_honeybadger_context).to eq(request_method: :post, request_url: "https://newsletter.example.com/posts", response_status: 422, response_body: "")`.
- When an action raises its own error in place of a service's error, check in the action spec's example for the service failing that the error's `cause` is the service's error and that its `to_honeybadger_context` is the cause's, e.g. `expect(error.cause).to be_a(NewsletterClient::Error)` and `expect(error.to_honeybadger_context).to eq(error.cause.to_honeybadger_context)` in the block passed to `raise_error(described_class::ServiceError)`. Stub the service to raise an error built with the details a real failure carries, e.g. `.and_raise(NewsletterClient::Error.new("Server error", status: 500))`.
- Give `HoneybadgerCauseContext` its own spec in `spec/models/concerns/honeybadger_cause_context_spec.rb`, with one example for a cause with context and one for a cause without it. Build an error class that includes the concern and raise it with `cause:`, e.g. `error_class = Class.new(StandardError) { include HoneybadgerCauseContext }` then `expect { raise error_class, cause: StandardError.new }.to raise_error(error_class) do |error|` and `expect(error.to_honeybadger_context).to eq({})`.
